0.0.n: A polite response, used here to begin speaking energetically.

1.0.n: A formal alternative to 今日, suitable for a workplace introduction.

1.1.n: Marks a starting time, more formally than から.

2.0.n: Politely refers to the branch where the speaker is introducing himself.

2.1.n: Links こちら to 支店, together meaning this branch.

2.2.n: Refers to a local office within a larger organization.

2.3.n: Marks the destination of the speaker’s assignment.

2.4.n: A noun for being placed in a particular department or office.

2.5.n: With なる, marks the resulting status: assignment to this branch.

2.6.n: Polite past form of なる; 配属となりました formally announces that the speaker has been assigned.

3.1.n: Marks the name being stated before 申します.

3.2.n: Polite form of 申す, a humble alternative to 言う used here to introduce oneself.

4.0.n: Part of a set introduction phrase asking for goodwill and a good working relationship.

4.1.n: The polite お attaches to 願い; together with いたします, it forms a respectful request.

4.2.n: Polite form of いたす, a humble alternative to する that makes the request especially courteous.

5.0.n: Before 大学, identifies the institution the speaker attended and graduated from.

5.1.n: 出身大学 refers to the university someone graduated from.

5.2.n: Marks the speaker’s university background as the topic.

5.3.n: 壱 means one, but here it forms part of the university name 壱松.

5.4.n: 松 means pine, but here it completes the university name 壱松.

5.5.n: Forms the institutional title in the name 壱松大学, Ichimatsu University.

5.6.n: The linking form of です or だ, connecting this statement to the next one.

6.0.n: Refers to the college where the speaker studied and played sports.

6.1.n: Marks the location where the football activity took place.

6.2.n: Added after で to frame university life as the topic.

6.3.n: A common abbreviation of アメリカンフットボール.

6.4.n: Marks アメフト as the activity performed with する.

6.5.n: 年間 expresses a duration measured in years; no extra particle is needed here.

6.6.n: して is the linking form of する; おりました is humble, polite past いる, describing an ongoing past activity.

7.0.n: Connects the previous football experience to the speaker’s confidence in his stamina.

7.1.n: Refers to the physical capacity and endurance the speaker gained through sports.

7.2.n: Marks what the speaker feels confident about in 自信がある.

7.3.n: Highlights stamina in particular as an area of confidence.

7.4.n: Used with がある to express being sure of one’s ability.

7.5.n: Marks 自信 as the thing the speaker has.

7.6.n: Polite form of ある; 自信があります expresses having confidence.

7.7.n: Presents the speaker’s confidence as the reason for the following request.

7.9.n: Combines with でも to form 何でも, expressing unrestricted choice.

7.10.n: Part of でも in 何でも; it does not independently mark a location or means here.

7.11.n: Completes 何でも, emphasizing that no particular task is excluded.

7.12.n: やらせて comes from やらせる, the let-or-make form of やる; ください turns it into a request for permission.

0.tip: はい is polite and can also signal readiness to speak.

1.tip: より marks the starting point and sounds more formal than から.

2.lit: To this branch, assignment has become.
2.tip: 配属となりました is a formal way to say you have been assigned somewhere.

3.tip: Name + と申します is a humble, professional way to introduce yourself.

4.tip: This set phrase asks for goodwill; in introductions, natural English often uses pleased to meet you.

5.lit: As for my university of graduation, it is Ichimatsu University, and…
5.tip: The final で links a statement ending in a noun to the next statement.

6.lit: At university, American football for four years I was doing.
6.tip: しておりました is a humble, polite version of していました, appropriate in a formal introduction.

7.lit: So, regarding stamina, because I have confidence, please let me do anything.
7.tip: やらせてください requests permission to do something, rather than asking someone else to do it.
